About the Medical Spelling event

Medical Spelling is a Health Science event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: testing.

Ten in-depth lessons for both rounds of HOSA Medical Spelling: the 50-item multiple-choice test and the oral spelldown. Lessons teach the word-part rules, letter patterns, plurals and sound-alikes behind thousands of terms, with a spelling studio that marks each letter, word builders, drills and spelldown simulations. Spellings follow standard U.S. usage; the official references are Taber’s Cyclopedic Medical Dictionary and Taber’s Audio Glossary, which you should use for pronunciation practice.

Medical Spelling lessons

Unit 1 · The event and the building blocks

Round One and Round Two rules, study methods, and the rules that join roots, prefixes and suffixes.

  1. The Medical Spelling event and a study system that works 25 min

    Medical Spelling has two very different rounds. In the first, you recognize the correct spelling among near-misses on paper. In the second, you stand before judges, hear a term from an audio glossary and spell it aloud…

  2. Roots, combining vowels and the rules that join word parts 25 min

    Why is it gastritis and not gastroitis, but gastroscopy and not gastrscopy? Medical words are assembled from parts, and a small set of joining rules decides when the combining vowel stays and when it drops. Learn the…

  3. Prefixes and suffixes that are easy to confuse 25 min

    Hypo- and hyper- differ by one letter and mean opposite things. Gastrectomy removes the stomach; gastrotomy only cuts into it; gastrostomy creates an opening. Near-identical word parts produce many of the hardest Round…

Unit 2 · Spelling patterns and traps

Greek letter patterns, silent letters, doubled letters, vowel order, plurals and adjective forms.

  1. Greek letter patterns: silent letters and unusual beginnings 25 min

    Pneumonia begins with a silent p. Psychiatry begins with ps. Rhinitis hides an h after its r, and xerostomia starts with an x that sounds like z. Greek-derived spellings preserve letters English speakers no longer…

  2. Doubled letters, vowel order and other sequence traps 25 min

    Accommodation, occlusion, appendicitis, staphylococcus, abscess—each contains a doubled letter that spellers often drop, and each has a neighbor that does not double. Sequence errors are the most common kind of…

  3. Greek and Latin plurals, adjectives and related forms 25 min

    One vertebra, two vertebrae. One bacterium, many bacteria. One diagnosis, several diagnoses. Medical plurals follow the rules of the languages the words came from, and spelling lists test them because English…

Unit 3 · Meaning and body-system vocabulary

Sound-alikes and look-alikes, then high-frequency terms from every body system.

  1. Sound-alikes and look-alikes 25 min

    Ileum and ilium sound identical, but one is part of the small intestine and the other part of the hip bone. Perineal, peroneal and peritoneal differ by a few letters and refer to three different regions. Many of the…

  2. Cardiovascular, respiratory and digestive vocabulary 25 min

    Sphygmomanometer, bronchiectasis, esophagogastroduodenoscopy: the circulatory, respiratory and digestive systems contribute some of the longest and most frequently misspelled terms. Breaking them into body-system parts…

  3. Nervous, musculoskeletal, endocrine, urinary and reproductive vocabulary 25 min

    Glomerulonephritis, myasthenia gravis, pheochromocytoma, oophorectomy: the remaining body systems add roots that look nothing like everyday English. Learning the roots once lets you spell dozens of terms across…

Unit 4 · Advanced terms and the spelldown

Eponyms, multiword and complicated terms, and competition performance.

  1. Eponyms, multiword terms and spelldown performance 25 min

    Guillain-Barré syndrome requires a hyphen and an accent. Alzheimer disease may appear with or without an apostrophe. Myasthenia gravis is two words. In the spelldown, you must say “hyphen,” “space” and “apostrophe”…

Sample Medical Spelling questions

1. A low level of potassium in the blood

  1. hypokalemia
  2. hypocalemia
  3. hypokalamia
  4. hypokalimia
Show answer

A. hypokalemia

The correct spelling is “hypokalemia.” Hypo- (below) + kal/i (potassium, from Latin kalium) + -emia (blood condition). The k comes from kalium.

2. Drooping of the upper eyelid

  1. tosis
  2. ptosys
  3. ptosis
  4. ptossis
Show answer

C. ptosis

The correct spelling is “ptosis.” From Greek ptosis (a falling). The p is silent but required.

3. Surgical repair or reshaping of the nose

  1. rinoplasty
  2. rhinoplasty
  3. rhinoplastie
  4. rhynoplasty
Show answer

B. rhinoplasty

The correct spelling is “rhinoplasty.” Rhin/o (nose) + -plasty (surgical repair). Rhin/o begins with “rh.”
